lessons.title: A feeling in colour or sound
lessons.outcome: Use colour/sound to express a feeling.
lessons.goal: I can use a colour or sound to show a feeling.
success: I can choose a feeling for my art.
I can try two marks or sounds.
I can show my choice in my arts log.
words: How a person might feel, such as calm or glad.
A dot, line or shape you make.
A steady pulse you can tap or show.
Something you pick for a reason.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: You can point, speak, sign or pass.
Choose a made-up feeling: calm or full of energy.
You do not need to tell a story about your life.
stages.say: We can make art about a made-up feeling. Pick calm or full of energy, or use another word. You can show your choice in silence.
stages.good: A pupil chooses or confirms a feeling. There is no demand for personal disclosure.
stages.fallback: Point left for calm or right for energy. Confirm the choice aloud without interpreting it.
stages.answer: Both choices are valid. Accept a pupil's own feeling word and any culturally different colour association.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Watch a slow hand wave. Watch two quick hand taps.
Which might show calm?
Can someone choose the other one? Say or show why.
stages.say: I move slowly, then I tap twice. I think the slow move could show calm. Your idea may differ if you can show a reason.
stages.good: The pupil links a feature such as speed or space to a feeling. An alternative interpretation is accepted.
stages.fallback: Use just silent hand movements. Pupils may watch or direct the adult with one or two fingers.
stages.answer: A slow wave might show calm because it moves gently. Quick taps could show calm for someone who enjoys a steady beat. Meaning depends on the maker.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch two tiny tests.
Colour: try a smooth line, then short marks.
Sound: try a slow soft beat, then a faster beat.
Pick one way to work. You do not need to do both.
stages.say: My made-up feeling is calm. I try a smooth blue line. Next I try short blue marks. I choose the smooth line because it flows. For sound I try four slow soft taps, pause, then four quicker taps. I prefer slow taps for my calm piece. These are my choices, not rules.
stages.good: The adult models two tests and a reason. Show that another colour, silence or different marks can express the same feeling.
stages.fallback: Trace a smooth line in the air and show short silent taps with the fingers. The pupil can direct the adult's hand movement.
stages.answer: The key is an intentional choice and reason. Blue does not always mean calm. Quiet sound is an option, and silence is a valid artistic choice.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Choose calm or energy for a class test.
Tell the adult: slow or fast? Smooth or short?
Try two versions. Keep one.
Finish: We chose ___ because ___.
stages.say: You choose the feeling. I will change only the speed or the marks. Which version fits your idea? Point to the choice, then I will read your reason back.
stages.good: Every pupil makes a choice. The class compares two deliberate versions and gives a feature-based reason. The adult does not supply the pupil's feeling.
stages.fallback: Make two silent hand paths. The pupil can point to a version or direct a partner, with adult confirmation.
stages.answer: For example: We chose slow marks because they feel still. Accept a different reason if it links a visible or heard feature to the intended effect.

stages.name: Create
pupil: In your book or arts log, choose a feeling.
Try two tiny colour tests or two sound tests.
Keep one and make a short piece.
Say or show: I chose ___ because ___.
Keep your tests. You can ask an adult to write your words.
stages.say: Work in paint or sound. With paint, try two small marks on scrap before your piece. Keep water and paint on the mat. With sound, tap softly below talking volume, use four beats and a pause, and stop on my raised hand. Choose silence if sound is too much. Point to the version you keep and tell me why.
stages.good: A short painting or sound pattern with two genuine trials, a pupil choice and a reason. A simple piece is complete for this lesson. An adult may handle materials under the pupil's direction.
stages.fallback: Use a silent four-move finger pattern or an air drawing. A pupil may direct the adult. The adult records the sequence and exact confirmed words on the supplied log. No materials or device is needed for participation.
stages.answer: Example sound piece: four slow soft taps, a pause, repeated once. Example painting: spaced curved blue marks. Each is a teacher model, not a required answer or pupil evidence.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Stop and put tools down.
Show one mark, beat or pause that you chose.
Your partner says: I notice ___.
Tidy your space. You can share with just the adult.
stages.say: Tell the maker one thing you notice, not what they must be feeling. Ask: Is that the feeling you chose? Listen to their answer. We have two minutes to cap paint, wipe the mat and leave the piece flat to dry. Keep each pupil's tests for next lesson.
stages.good: A respectful observation linked to a feature and a maker's confirmed intention. Tools are secure and work is stored flat. The pupil may share privately.
stages.fallback: The adult repeats a silent pattern and asks the pupil to confirm one feature. No peer audience is required today.
stages.answer: A useful observation is: I notice big gaps between the marks. A guess about a pupil's private life is not required or recorded.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: Arts log: I tried ___.
I chose ___ because ___.
Next time I will ___.
Point to, sketch or describe your real work.
stages.say: Show what you actually made or tried. I can write your words, read them back and let you change them. Our log keeps your idea and one real next step. You may say the piece is still a test.
stages.good: A dated arts-log entry records the form, trial, chosen feature and reason. Staff record the support actually used. No model answer is entered as pupil evidence.
stages.fallback: Pupil confirms a choice by gesture. Adult makes a short witnessed record and reads it back at the next available recording opportunity.
stages.answer: Example only: I tried two beats. I chose slow taps because I wanted calm. Next time I will add a pause.

Supported: Pick calm or energy, or point to your own word.
Try two lines or beats with an adult.
Choose one. Direct the adult if you want.
Independent: Choose a feeling and paint or sound.
Try two small versions. Keep both tests.
Make a short piece with your choice.
Add your choice and reason to your arts log.
Aspire: Change one feature, such as space, speed or a pause.
Say how the new version changes the feeling.
Keep your own reason in your arts log.

log: My art form is paint / sound / silent movement.
misconceptions: One colour always means one feeling
Ask the maker what the colour means to them. Accept different personal and cultural meanings.
Loud sound is needed to show energy
Use faster quiet taps, silent movement or a pause. All work stays below talking volume.
A neat picture is the only good outcome
Look for an intentional choice and a reason. Marks or a brief sound pattern can express an idea.
kit: For four pupils: four books or arts logs and four pencils.
Painting option: five small sheets, mats, five brushes, a small shared set of washable paint and one stable water pot per pair. Prepare two adult test swatches.
Sound option: hands or fingertips, no instrument or recording device required. Use soft knee taps only if comfortable.
Six scrap pieces for tests, drying space and cloths. Keep wet materials away from electrical items.
No-materials option: silent hand patterns or pupil-directed adult movement.
demo: 0 to 15 seconds
Say: My made-up feeling is calm. Draw one long curve in the air.
15 to 30 seconds
Show short marks. Say: I tried two ways. I choose the curve because it flows.
30 to 45 seconds
Tap four soft slow beats, pause, then four quicker beats. Say: I can test sound too.
45 to 60 seconds
Point to the chosen test. Say: I keep my real choice and reason in my log.
models: Teacher model only: My feeling is calm. I tried short marks and a long curve. I chose the curve because it flows.
Teacher model only: I made four quick soft taps, then a pause. My piece shows energy without loud noise.

lessons.title: My feelings piece and arts log
lessons.outcome: Use colour/sound to express a feeling.
lessons.goal: I can make a short piece and tell you about my choice.
success: I can find my test and chosen feeling.
I can use a mark or sound on purpose.
I can add my work and words to my arts log.
words: How a person might feel, such as calm or glad.
A short time with no sound or move.
Look or listen again and say what you notice.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Find your test from last time.
Point to the mark or beat you chose.
You may keep the feeling or choose a new one.
stages.say: Find your own tests. If you were away, we can make two tiny tests now. We keep today's real date and say what happened. A feeling can be made up.
stages.good: The pupil identifies a real previous choice or makes a short honest catch-up trial. No earlier evidence is invented.
stages.fallback: Adult recalls only a choice that was actually witnessed. If none exists, offer two silent patterns to try now.
stages.answer: Either continuing or making a fresh trial is valid. Log the actual work and date.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Watch four soft taps with a pause.
Watch the same taps with no pause.
What changed? Which version fits your idea?
stages.say: The taps stay soft. This time I change only the pause. Show me what changed and tell me which you would choose for a made-up feeling.
stages.good: The pupil identifies the pause and makes an intentional choice, rather than copying an expected feeling.
stages.fallback: Use four silent finger moves, hold still, repeat. Pupils may just watch and point.
stages.answer: The pause changed. It might create calm, waiting or surprise. The maker's reason determines the intended effect.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch a tiny piece grow from a test.
Paint: repeat a chosen mark.
Sound: repeat a four-beat pattern.
I can keep a choice or change it.
stages.say: I use yesterday's curve test to make three spaced curves. I keep the space because I want calm. If I choose sound, I repeat four soft taps and a pause twice. I check my idea, then keep a sketch or a beat plan and my own words. These are adult examples.
stages.good: A clear link from trial to piece, one deliberate feature and a short review. The piece can stay small. Show how to log a sound using written beat words or simple dots and a gap.
stages.fallback: Make three air curves or a silent four-move sequence. Say what an adult could record as a witnessed performance.
stages.answer: The log may contain a sketch, written pattern, work-only image or witnessed description. A recording device is not needed.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Help make a class piece for a made-up character.
Pick one mark or four-beat pattern.
Try a change. Choose keep or change.
Finish: We chose ___ because ___.
stages.say: Our made-up character feels hopeful. You direct my marks or soft taps. We can change the space or add a pause. Which should we keep and why? Each pupil's own work comes next.
stages.good: Pupils test one small change and confirm an intention. The shared class model is labelled as a model and is separate from individual evidence.
stages.fallback: Adult follows pupils' silent hand directions. Use a gesture for keep or change.
stages.answer: For example: We kept the growing gaps because they feel open. Other justified choices are valid. Hope does not have one fixed colour or sound.

stages.name: Create
pupil: Use your test to make a small painting or sound piece.
Repeat your mark or short pattern.
Check one feature. Keep it or change it.
Keep a sketch, beat plan or adult witness note.
Add: I chose ___ because ___.
stages.say: Choose paint, sound or the silent option. Use your own idea. Make it small enough to finish a first version today. Check one feature, then keep or change it for a reason. I can move materials under your direction. Sound stays below talking volume and stops on my raised hand.
stages.good: A real first piece or clearly labelled unfinished work, a deliberate feature, a keep/change decision and pupil-owned log. Adult help supports access without supplying the choice.
stages.fallback: Create a silent hand sequence or air drawing, or direct the adult. Record the order, intended feeling and confirmed reason on the arts-log sheet when available.
stages.answer: A complete lesson response may be four soft taps and a pause repeated twice, with a simple beat plan and reason. A painting can use only a few intentional marks.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Show your work to an adult or partner.
Say: I chose ___ because ___.
Listener: I notice ___.
Tidy and store your work.
stages.say: Ask the maker before you comment. Describe a mark, sound or pause, then let the maker explain. You can share privately. We use the last two minutes to wipe mats, cap paint and place work flat. Keep the maker's own review.
stages.good: The maker explains one feature and receives a respectful observation. No compulsory performance or personal disclosure. Work and evidence remain individual.
stages.fallback: The adult watches a silent sequence and reads a short description back for pupil approval. A private audience is enough today.
stages.answer: For example: I chose a long pause because the character is waiting. I notice the pause comes after each four taps.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: Arts log: I made ___.
I chose ___ because ___.
I kept or changed ___.
Next I would like to ___.
stages.say: Your log can be spoken, drawn or written. I will scribe your exact words and read them back if needed. Show the work or plan the words refer to. Today contributes to your Explore record. We will keep building it across the term.
stages.good: A dated entry links actual work with the pupil's intention, decision and next step. Staff state what was witnessed and what help was used, without claiming the whole award is complete.
stages.fallback: Pupil confirms the sequence and reason using gestures. Adult records that response, with the actual support and date, at the next recording opportunity.
stages.answer: Example only: I made a calm sound piece. I kept slow taps because they feel still. Next I would like to try two sounds.

Supported: Find your test. Choose a mark or beat.
Make a tiny piece with an adult if needed.
Point to one part to keep or change.
Tell or show your choice for the log.
Independent: Make a small piece from your chosen test.
Review it. Keep or change one thing and say why.
Add your work and words to the arts log.
Aspire: Complete the core piece and log.
Try one part in a new way.
Explain which version fits your idea best.
Keep the test and your reason, even if you keep the first version.

log: My work or witness record is ___.
misconceptions: Change means the first version failed
A trial helps the maker choose. Keeping a feature for a reason also counts as a review.
Only a recording can show a sound piece
Keep a simple beat plan and a dated witness description, confirmed by the pupil.
The audience decides the maker's feeling
Listeners describe what they notice. The maker explains the intended feeling.
kit: For four pupils: four previous tests, arts logs and pencils. Offer a catch-up test if a pupil was absent.
Paint option: four sheets, five brushes, mats, stable water pots, a small amount of washable paint and cloths.
Sound option: fingertips or quiet hand movement, no instrument required. Provide a quiet listening space.
Adult model: one test and one tiny developed example. Drying space for paintings.
No-materials option: silent finger sequence, air drawing or pupil-directed adult movement.
demo: 0 to 15 seconds
Point to a real adult test. Say: I choose this curve for calm.
15 to 30 seconds
Repeat three curves with spaces. Say: I keep space because it feels still.
30 to 45 seconds
Show four soft taps and a pause twice. Say: I can show a sound in a beat plan.
45 to 60 seconds
Say: I kept this feature because it fits my idea. I keep my real work and words in my log.
models: Teacher model only: I made a small painting. I chose spaced curves for calm. I kept the gaps because they feel still.
Teacher model only: I made a sound piece with four taps and a pause. I changed to a longer pause because the character is waiting.

lessons.title: Artists find different ways
lessons.outcome: Explore how artists express resilience and change.
lessons.goal: Explore two descriptions of artists' work, test an artistic idea and plan a first response.
success: I identify a detail in a description of an artist's work.
I test repetition or a change in my chosen art form.
I explain one choice for my own response.
words: Your own art made after exploring an idea.
Finding a way forward. This can include a pause, help or a new method.
Using colour, shape or pattern without showing a realistic scene.

artist_cards.description: Henri Matisse made paintings and later developed cut-outs as artworks in their own right. Assistants painted paper. He cut shapes and directed their arrangement. The shapes could move while he tested an idea. This gives us a way to discuss changing a method and revising a design.
artist_cards.notice: What could Matisse change before the shapes were fixed?
artist_cards.prompt: How might moving a shape help an artist keep an idea going?
artist_cards.model_answer: He could change the positions or arrangement of the cut shapes. The artist can try a different position without starting everything again. I see this as one possible example of adapting.

artist_cards.description: Alma Thomas developed an abstract painting style using repeated coloured marks. Nature and space helped her find ideas. In The Eclipse, made in 1970, a dark blue centre sits within rings of colour. The centre is off to one side. This arrangement can suggest a moment of movement and change.
artist_cards.notice: Which two details does the description give us?
artist_cards.prompt: How could repeating marks help us show a change?
artist_cards.model_answer: A dark blue centre and surrounding rings of colour. The centre is off to one side. We could keep repeating a mark and gradually change its size, spacing or direction. This would be our own response, rather than a copy of the painting.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Choose marks, sound, movement or words. You can work quietly and share privately.
stages.say: You can use marks, sounds, movement or your own words. You can work quietly and show me privately. Our idea can be invented.
stages.good: The pupil chooses or indicates a form and knows the stop signal and quiet option.
stages.fallback: Point to or say an art form. Choose seated gestures or an original spoken description.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Repeat a small action. Change its size, pace or direction. What changed?
stages.say: What stayed the same? What changed? Repetition means doing something again. We can change pace, size, direction or space.
stages.good: The pupil notices one change or makes a simple repeat-and-change pattern.
stages.fallback: Use silent finger movements or describe 'small, small, larger'.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Listen to the artist descriptions. Find one detail in each. Watch the original seed example.
stages.say: The description tells me that Matisse moved cut shapes while trying ideas. I think this method could help an artist adapt. That second statement is my interpretation. Thomas's work uses repeated marks. My seed will use repetition in a different design.
stages.good: The pupil can point to or repeat a verified detail and hears the difference between a fact and a personal reading.
stages.fallback: Read both cards aloud and model a silent repeat-and-change gesture. No image, internet or art materials are needed.
stages.answer: Which is a detail from the description: 'Thomas used rings of colour' or 'Everyone must feel happy'? Expected: rings of colour.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Try two versions with a partner or adult. Which version fits your idea? Say why.
Hinge: an idea is unclear. Should the artist copy, change one feature and test, or give up?
stages.say: What can move or change? Try version one, pause, then try version two. Which version suggests your chosen idea, and why? You can disagree politely. An artist wants to keep the idea of growth but the first attempt is unclear. Should they A copy every shape from a famous work, B change one feature and try again, or C stop because art must be perfect? Explain your choice.
stages.good: The pupil tests two versions and gives a reason linked to a feature, such as wider spacing, slower pace or an upward direction. The pupil selects B and links an adjustment to the idea. The teacher rereads and models one change if the pupil selects A or C.
stages.fallback: Direct the adult's hand positions, or perform two seated gestures. Say the two versions if movement is uncomfortable. Choose A, B or C verbally or by pointing. Describe the first and last part of a planned gesture or sound pattern.
stages.answer: If the pupil cannot explain B, model changing only spacing, then use a parallel hinge: 'A quiet sound idea feels too busy. Would fewer taps and a pause help test the idea?' Continue independently when the pupil identifies a purposeful change.

stages.name: Create
pupil: Make a small first response about resilience or change. Use your own subject.
Repeat a feature. Change one thing. You may pause or ask for help.
stages.say: Use your own idea. Show something continuing through a change. You may use colour and shape, an original sound pattern, a short movement or your own words. Stop after a small first version.
stages.good: The pupil makes or directs a first attempt with a clear repeated feature and a deliberate change. The work need not be neat or finished.
stages.fallback: Create and repeat a short silent gesture sequence, or speak an original description. Adult records the action sequence and the pupil's stated choice.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Share privately or with a partner. Explain one artist link. Add your choice to the arts log.
stages.say: Which artist's method or idea helped you? What did you choose for your own work? What might you test next time? You can say 'This suggests ... to me'.
stages.good: The log links an artist detail to a pupil choice and identifies one next test. The adult distinguishes the pupil's words from a staff observation.
stages.fallback: Give an oral log. Adult retains a dated note of the artist detail, pupil choice and observed first attempt. If recording is unavailable, repeat the pattern with the adult and note it later.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: Choose one part to keep and one thing to test next time.
stages.say: Next time you will develop this first response. Which part will you keep? What is one thing you might adjust? A pause or help can be part of the plan.
stages.good: The pupil identifies one feature to retain or change. Materials are put away calmly.
stages.fallback: Agree a short spoken cue to remember the sequence. Adult records its ordered steps and next test.

Supported: Choose Matisse's movable shapes or Thomas's repeated marks from two spoken descriptions. Use an adult's model for the first repeat, then choose your own change. Say, point or dictate: 'I chose ... because ...'.
Independent: Identify a detail from each artist card. Make two short trials in your chosen form, then choose one feature for your own first response and explain why.
Aspire: Try the same idea in two forms. You could use marks, then gestures. Choose one form. Say why it fits your idea. The next level task is optional.

log: An artist detail I noticed was ...
misconceptions: Everyone reads a colour or sound in the same way.
Colours and sounds can suggest different feelings to different people. A reasoned personal reading is valid.
Resilience means doing the same thing until it works.
An artist can change a method, take a break or ask for help. A purposeful adjustment counts.
A response must copy the artist's work.
Borrow an idea such as repetition or rearrangement, then make your own subject and design. Do not recreate an existing composition.
We know an artist's feelings just by describing a work.
Separate verified information from interpretation. Say 'This suggests ... to me' rather than claiming to know a private feeling.
kit: For five pupils: five books or arts logs, five pencils and ten small test sheets if available.
Optional visual route: five sheets, six brushes including the adult model, a small amount of familiar non-toxic paint, five mats, three stable water pots and cloths.
Optional collage route: ten scrap sheets and three glue sticks. Tear paper instead of cutting; no pins.
Movement, original words or quiet finger taps need no art materials. A pupil may direct the adult.
Keep the original work or a dated observation note and the pupil's confirmed words for lesson two.
demo: 0–15 seconds
Say: I want to show a seed growing after wind. Make four small grey zigzag marks, or four small sideways hand movements.
15–30 seconds
Say: I will repeat the movement, then change it. Add three green curves that grow taller, or move the hands slowly upwards.
30–45 seconds
Say: My last marks point up. That change suggests growth to me. Leave a pause and compare the first and last part.
45–60 seconds
Say: I can test another spacing or pace. I will choose the version that best fits my idea. This is our original example, not a copy of an artwork.

stretch.label: Optional next level stretch
stretch.task: Use both artist cards. Note one fact about each artist. Say which method interests you. Give your reason. Set one skill to practise. You can draw, speak or write.
stretch.evidence: Keep both facts, your view and reason, and your skill goal. Say which card you used. An adult can write your words.
stretch.why_optional: Additional evidence may support later work at the next level. It is optional and is not needed for this lesson's Explore success criteria. The owner must review any future level requirements.
stretch.good: The pupil distinguishes description from personal view, compares rearrangement with repetition and explains a choice for future practice.
stretch.fallback: Adult asks the same prompts and records a dated note using the pupil's own words.

models: Matisse could move shapes to test a design. I moved my curved marks so the seed seemed to grow upwards. I kept the spaces small at first, then made them wider. Next time I will test fewer marks so the change is clearer.
lessons.cover: Read the two short artist cards aloud. Ask pupils to repeat and change a silent hand movement. Model the seed example using words and gestures. Pupils make their own repeat-and-change response, explain one artist link and complete an oral or written log. Use the seven-stage timings. No artwork display or internet is required. Reserve the final two minutes of Review for quiet tidy-up and safe storage. If the previous response is missing, make a fresh short trial and record today's actual date.

staff_guidance.plain_language: Resilience can include pausing, asking for help, changing a method and trying again. It does not mean hiding feelings, tolerating harm or working through pain.
staff_guidance.scope: This week's Explore learning and evidence are complete without the optional stretch tasks. Completing these lessons does not itself confer an award. The optional tasks retain additional research, reflection and skills evidence which the owner can review if the level changes later.
staff_guidance.art_specialist_help: You do not need to paint or perform expertly. Model the decision, a small first attempt and one change. Assess the pupil's choice and explanation rather than a polished result. A pupil may use visual art, original sound, movement, drama or original words.
staff_guidance.sensory_and_emotional_access: Offer a quiet visual or silent gesture route before any sound. Keep sound at speaking level and stop together on an agreed open-hand signal. No sudden sounds, flashing images, blindfolds or personal disclosure. Work seated if preferred. Use an invented situation, such as a seed growing after wind. Pupils may pass on public sharing and show work privately to a trusted adult. Agree a calm-space and return cue before starting.
staff_guidance.safety: Use non-toxic familiar materials. Check sensory and access needs. Follow local procedures for scissors and paint. Tearing or drawing can replace cutting. No pins are used. A pupil directs an adult to position shapes if needed. Do not recreate illness or treat an artist's health as a moral lesson.
prompt_ladder: Point to the instruction or place.
Model the first step only, then return the task.

adaptations.cognition_and_learning: Read one artist card at a time. Pre-teach repeat, change, method and response. Offer two concrete choices, then fade the choice prompt.
adaptations.communication_and_interaction: Allow pointing, a gesture, a short spoken response or an adult scribe. Give processing time before asking again. Use 'I notice ... I think ... because ...'.
adaptations.semh: Use fictional or abstract themes. Let the pupil choose the art form and audience. Treat a pause or change of approach as a valid creative decision.
adaptations.sensory_and_physical: Provide a silent route, seated movement, large marks and directed placement. Ask consent before touching work. Separate observation from performance demands.
adaptations.eal: Plan in any language. Teach repeat and change with gestures. Accept a labelled sketch or oral explanation before a fuller sentence. Check meaning rather than accent or spelling.

misconceptions.claim: Everyone reads a colour or sound in the same way.
misconceptions.correction: Colours and sounds can suggest different feelings to different people. A reasoned personal reading is valid.

misconceptions.claim: Resilience means doing the same thing until it works.
misconceptions.correction: An artist can change a method, take a break or ask for help. A purposeful adjustment counts.

misconceptions.claim: A response must copy the artist's work.
misconceptions.correction: Borrow an idea such as repetition or rearrangement, then make your own subject and design. Do not recreate an existing composition.

misconceptions.claim: We know an artist's feelings just by describing a work.
misconceptions.correction: Separate verified information from interpretation. Say 'This suggests ... to me' rather than claiming to know a private feeling.

staff_guidance.careers_line: Artists, designers and performers try ideas, respond to feedback and explain creative choices.

cold_call.foundation: Which detail can you find in the description?
cold_call.middle: How could moving or repeating a feature change its effect?
cold_call.higher: Which part is a fact, and which part is your interpretation?

ta_focus.I do: Point to the detail being read. Allow processing time. Avoid replacing an interpretation with your own.
ta_focus.We do: Prompt one change at a time. Ask the pupil to direct a version rather than completing it for them.
ta_focus.Independent: Record help accurately. After modelling the first step, return the choice and the next action to the pupil.

lessons.evidence: Retain the first attempt or a precise adult observation of a live response, plus the arts-log entry. Record art form, artist link, chosen feature and support used. A photograph or recording is optional and follows local consent procedures. No pupil names are needed in the supplied template.
lessons.artist_use_note: Use the descriptions and original classroom examples. No reproduced artwork, lyrics or artist quotation is supplied. Pupils borrow a general method, then make their own design.

lessons.title: A first response to change
lessons.outcome: Explore how artists express resilience and change.
lessons.goal: I can develop my first response, test a change and record how an artist's idea helped me.
success: I make or direct an original response to resilience or change.
I test one adjustment and describe its effect.
I add evidence and a personal view to my arts log.
words: Your own art made after exploring an idea.
Finding a way forward. This can include a pause, help or a new method.
Using colour, shape or pattern without showing a realistic scene.

artist_cards.description: Henri Matisse made paintings and later developed cut-outs as artworks in their own right. Assistants painted paper. He cut shapes and directed their arrangement. The shapes could move while he tested an idea. This gives us a way to discuss changing a method and revising a design.
artist_cards.notice: What could Matisse change before the shapes were fixed?
artist_cards.prompt: How might moving a shape help an artist keep an idea going?
artist_cards.model_answer: He could change the positions or arrangement of the cut shapes. The artist can try a different position without starting everything again. I see this as one possible example of adapting.

artist_cards.description: Alma Thomas developed an abstract painting style using repeated coloured marks. Nature and space helped her find ideas. In The Eclipse, made in 1970, a dark blue centre sits within rings of colour. The centre is off to one side. This arrangement can suggest a moment of movement and change.
artist_cards.notice: Which two details does the description give us?
artist_cards.prompt: How could repeating marks help us show a change?
artist_cards.model_answer: A dark blue centre and surrounding rings of colour. The centre is off to one side. We could keep repeating a mark and gradually change its size, spacing or direction. This would be our own response, rather than a copy of the painting.

stages.name: Arrival
pupil: Recall your first response. You may keep the art form or change your method.
stages.say: Last time you tried an idea. You may keep that form or change your method. Let us check the quiet option and stop signal before we begin.
stages.good: The pupil recognises a previous choice or chooses a manageable restart.
stages.fallback: Adult reads the ordered note. Pupil repeats or directs the previous gesture or spoken sequence.

stages.name: Starter
pupil: Recall one detail about Matisse and one about Thomas. Listen to the cards again if needed.
stages.say: Which artist tested arrangements of cut shapes? Which artist used repeated coloured marks? You can listen to the cards again.
stages.good: The pupil identifies an artist feature, with rereading if needed.
stages.fallback: Use the spoken cards and two verbal choices. Point to a numbered choice or answer orally.

stages.name: I do
pupil: Watch one change to the original seed example. What changed? Why?
stages.say: My first marks all point sideways. I want growth to be clearer, so I change the last marks to point up. I keep the first part. This is my interpretation of resilience. The artists helped me think about a method, but this design is my own.
stages.good: The pupil notices a specific before-and-after change and hears a reason linked to the idea.
stages.fallback: Use the same seated gesture sequence, changing only its final direction. Describe it if movement is uncomfortable.
stages.answer: Did I change a feature for a reason, or only add more? Expected: changed the final direction to suggest growth.

stages.name: We do
pupil: Try two versions of one feature. Ask what your partner notices.
Hinge: must you use feedback, ignore it, or consider it and choose for your purpose?
stages.say: Let us try both versions. Tell me what you notice before suggesting a change. You can say 'The second version seems ... because ...'. The artist chooses what to keep. A listener says, 'The slow ending feels steady to me.' Must the artist A use that opinion, B ignore it, or C consider it and choose a change for their own purpose? Explain.
stages.good: The pupil compares two versions and hears feedback linked to a visible or audible feature. They retain control of the choice. The pupil selects C and explains that feedback helps a decision but does not remove their choice.
stages.fallback: Perform two quiet or silent versions. The adult describes observed pace, spacing or direction without judging personal feelings. Choose from the spoken options and say or indicate one feature to test.
stages.answer: If the pupil selects A or B without a reason, model two different interpretations and reread the purpose. Parallel hinge: 'Two people read blue differently. Can the artist keep blue and explain their intention?' Expected: yes. Move on when the pupil chooses a feature for a reason.

stages.name: Create
pupil: Develop your own response. Test one change. Choose the version to keep.
Use a quiet or silent route if you prefer. You may pause or ask for help.
stages.say: Make the response manageable. Use repetition or rearrangement in your own way. Keep the first version in a note or memory cue, test one change, then decide what to keep.
stages.good: The pupil creates or directs a short original response and makes one purposeful adjustment. Art form may change when it improves access or suits the idea.
stages.fallback: Use a silent gesture, short drama sequence, original sound pattern or spoken piece. Adult observes before and after and records the exact ordered actions and pupil's reason.

stages.name: Review
pupil: Explain the artist link and your own choices. Record your change and its effect in the arts log.
stages.say: What idea did you borrow from an artist's method? What did you make yourself? Which change helped, and how do you know? You can explain that different viewers may read it differently.
stages.good: The pupil identifies a genuine artist link, describes their own choice and evaluates a specific adjustment.
stages.fallback: Adult records a brief dated oral log. Separate the pupil's stated intention from the adult's observation.

stages.name: Exit
pupil: Choose one next step. Keep your response and log evidence together.
stages.say: What did you learn about making art through change? Choose one next step, such as more practice, a different material or asking for feedback. You can be satisfied with a small response today.
stages.good: The pupil gives a specific next step. The retained record shows participation, exploration and a view of their own work.
stages.fallback: Say the next step while the adult repeats it back and records it with the observed response.

Supported: Choose one change from two options. Adult models only its first step. Make or direct the rest and complete 'I changed ... It helped because ...' orally or through a scribe.
Independent: Make your first response. Test one change. Choose which version to keep. Say how an artist's method helped you.
Aspire: Use two features in your piece. Say how they work together. How might someone else read your art? Keep or change a feature. Say why. The next level task is optional.

log: The artist idea I explored was ...
Before, I ... After my test, I ...
misconceptions: Everyone reads a colour or sound in the same way.
Colours and sounds can suggest different feelings to different people. A reasoned personal reading is valid.
Resilience means doing the same thing until it works.
An artist can change a method, take a break or ask for help. A purposeful adjustment counts.
A response must copy the artist's work.
Borrow an idea such as repetition or rearrangement, then make your own subject and design. Do not recreate an existing composition.
We know an artist's feelings just by describing a work.
Separate verified information from interpretation. Say 'This suggests ... to me' rather than claiming to know a private feeling.
kit: For five pupils: five books or arts logs, five pencils and ten small test sheets if available.
Optional visual route: five sheets, six brushes including the adult model, a small amount of familiar non-toxic paint, five mats, three stable water pots and cloths.
Optional collage route: ten scrap sheets and three glue sticks. Tear paper instead of cutting; no pins.
Movement, original words or quiet finger taps need no art materials. A pupil may direct the adult.
Keep the original work or a dated observation note and the pupil's confirmed words for lesson two.
demo: 0–15 seconds
Say: I want to show a seed growing after wind. Make four small grey zigzag marks, or four small sideways hand movements.
15–30 seconds
Say: I will repeat the movement, then change it. Add three green curves that grow taller, or move the hands slowly upwards.
30–45 seconds
Say: My last marks point up. That change suggests growth to me. Leave a pause and compare the first and last part.
45–60 seconds
Say: I can test another spacing or pace. I will choose the version that best fits my idea. This is our original example, not a copy of an artwork.

stretch.label: Optional next level stretch
stretch.task: Set one skill goal. Keep a note of your first try. Practise that skill. Try your piece again. Compare the two versions. Say how an artist's method helped. What feedback did you use? Choose your next practice step.
stretch.evidence: Keep your goal, both versions or a witness note, and your views. Add your artist link, feedback used and next step.
stretch.why_optional: This retains additional evidence for possible future progression. It does not change the lesson level or make the Explore work dependent on stretch completion.
stretch.good: The pupil identifies how practising one skill changed the response and evaluates the change against their own intention rather than simply saying it is better.
stretch.fallback: Adult observes both live versions and records the ordered actions with the pupil's explanation. Audio, image and written pupil work are not required.

models: Thomas's repeated marks helped me think about repeating a gesture. My movement begins with small curved hands and gradually rises. I tried a sudden jump at the end, then a slow rise. I kept the slow rise because it suggests steady growth to me. Someone else may read it differently. Next I will practise the pauses.
lessons.cover: Recover the previous response from the work or adult note. Model one change to the seed example. Pupils test a single adjustment, choose what to keep and log the artist link and effect. Accept silent or spoken work and private sharing. Optional stretch can be omitted. Reserve the final two minutes of Review for quiet tidy-up and safe storage. If the previous response is missing, make a fresh short trial and record today's actual date.

staff_guidance.plain_language: Resilience can include pausing, asking for help, changing a method and trying again. It does not mean hiding feelings, tolerating harm or working through pain.
staff_guidance.scope: This week's Explore learning and evidence are complete without the optional stretch tasks. Completing these lessons does not itself confer an award. The optional tasks retain additional research, reflection and skills evidence which the owner can review if the level changes later.
staff_guidance.art_specialist_help: You do not need to paint or perform expertly. Model the decision, a small first attempt and one change. Assess the pupil's choice and explanation rather than a polished result. A pupil may use visual art, original sound, movement, drama or original words.
staff_guidance.sensory_and_emotional_access: Offer a quiet visual or silent gesture route before any sound. Keep sound at speaking level and stop together on an agreed open-hand signal. No sudden sounds, flashing images, blindfolds or personal disclosure. Work seated if preferred. Use an invented situation, such as a seed growing after wind. Pupils may pass on public sharing and show work privately to a trusted adult. Agree a calm-space and return cue before starting.
staff_guidance.safety: Use non-toxic familiar materials. Check sensory and access needs. Follow local procedures for scissors and paint. Tearing or drawing can replace cutting. No pins are used. A pupil directs an adult to position shapes if needed. Do not recreate illness or treat an artist's health as a moral lesson.
prompt_ladder: Point to the instruction or place.
Model the first step only, then return the task.

adaptations.cognition_and_learning: Read one artist card at a time. Pre-teach repeat, change, method and response. Offer two concrete choices, then fade the choice prompt.
adaptations.communication_and_interaction: Allow pointing, a gesture, a short spoken response or an adult scribe. Give processing time before asking again. Use 'I notice ... I think ... because ...'.
adaptations.semh: Use fictional or abstract themes. Let the pupil choose the art form and audience. Treat a pause or change of approach as a valid creative decision.
adaptations.sensory_and_physical: Provide a silent route, seated movement, large marks and directed placement. Ask consent before touching work. Separate observation from performance demands.
adaptations.eal: Plan in any language. Teach repeat and change with gestures. Accept a labelled sketch or oral explanation before a fuller sentence. Check meaning rather than accent or spelling.

misconceptions.correction: Colours and sounds can suggest different feelings to different people. A reasoned personal reading is valid.

misconceptions.correction: Borrow an idea such as repetition or rearrangement, then make your own subject and design. Do not recreate an existing composition.

staff_guidance.careers_line: Artists, designers and performers try ideas, respond to feedback and explain creative choices.

cold_call.middle: What effect did your change have?
cold_call.higher: How could someone read the same response differently, and why did you keep your choice?

ta_focus.I do: Point out the one altered feature. Check that the pupil can identify before and after.
ta_focus.We do: Describe features rather than assigning a correct feeling. Protect the pupil's control over their response.
ta_focus.Independent: Fade prompts. Observe the chosen skill and support level. Keep the pupil's view distinct from your judgement.

lessons.evidence: Retain the response or precise live observation, the first-versus-revised comparison and the arts-log entry. Record artist link and support used. Optional stretch evidence is clearly labelled and stored separately from required Explore evidence.
lessons.artist_use_note: Use the descriptions and original classroom examples. No reproduced artwork, lyrics or artist quotation is supplied. Pupils borrow a general method, then make their own design.

scope: Both pathways work at Explore. Each lesson is complete without the optional GROW next level stretch. Week 1 contributes evidence towards the ongoing arts log and does not by itself complete an award. A description-based artist discussion is useful exploration but is not evidence of an unconfirmed live arts encounter.
timing: Arrival 0-3; Starter 3-6; I do 6-12; We do 12-18; Create 18-32; Review 32-37; Exit 37-40 minutes. Tidy in the final two minutes of Review.
